Such recalled states are associations reported by the same people at the same sitting, not predictors. An opinion piece by the same research group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, in one figure and without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same online survey (266 people who completed four surveys): readiness, a clear intention with strong expectations, and trust in the people who would be present, all rated before the experience, went with less challenging experiences; because it gives no measures, sample description or model details and its sample overlaps the prospective study's, it is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. Preparation is routine in clinical trials, but none of those reviewed compared different kinds of it: a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; it mapped what the trials reported, without appraising them or combining their outcomes), found that 21 described giving information about the effects, 19 meetings beforehand to build trust (mostly one to four, of about 2 hours each) and 18 advice on the attitude to take, mostly openness and letting go, and that no included trial compared different preparation, sets or settings; the review's remark that one trial's two-interview preparation made the experience and its benefits greater rests on a trial that did not vary preparation. Certainty: very low.

set.plain: People who felt calm, open and ready the day before a trip they had planned rated it as less difficult. In laboratory LSD sessions, feeling anxious beforehand went with more anxiety, while feeling well went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones. These links come from watching, not testing, and many people dropped out of the study outside the laboratory. Studies in which people recalled their mood afterwards found bigger links, but memories can be coloured by how the trip went. Clinical trials prepare people with meetings and advice beforehand, but a review of 25 trials found none that compared different ways of preparing.
set.grade.reasoning: Predictor studies start low, even inside randomized laboratory studies, because the predictors were not randomized; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated, for the direction only: more anxiety beforehand, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in two independent sources measured before the drug, one prospective and naturalistic (Imperial College London, the set component) and one laboratory (Basel, pre-dose anxiety), with different questionnaires, so it is a conceptual replication; recalled attributions in an independent panel (Simonsson et al.) point the same way. That a better mood goes with an easier experience rests on the naturalistic study alone: in the laboratory a better mood went with stronger effects overall. The other predictors rest on single studies or on states recalled afterwards. The review (Aday et al., 2021) is used only for what it adds (the retrospective Russ studies and the tabulation of absorption), since its Table 1 misprints the sign for set. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted as a further study or used for any figure (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2); and a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) shows only that no such trial up to December 2023 compared preparation, sets or settings. A randomized study in 75 healthy volunteers that varied the amount of preparation together with the dose and the support afterwards (Griffiths et al., 2018) is known here only from its description by Strickland et al. (2021) and has not been read.

No study compared settings by design. Certainty: very low.

An opinion piece by the same group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same survey (266 people who completed four surveys), in which a 'therapeutic setting' (how it was recorded is not given) went with more peak or mystical-type experiences and trust in the people who would be present, rated beforehand, with less challenging ones; in the prospective study above, which appears to be the fuller report, a similar rating of the people and the place showed only a non-significant trend and a retreat or therapeutic setting no statistically significant association, so the preview is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. No study read here put people in different places or company on purpose to compare them. The same opinion piece states that, by 2018 and apart from a dose study, retrospective analyses and one 1969 study, controlled studies isolating contextual factors had not been done, and a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023, found no trial that compared settings (Estric et al., 2025; the trials were not appraised); in those trials, 12 kept two staff in the room throughout the session and five, published in 2023, one per participant, and rooms ranged from a hospital room left unchanged (4 trials) to one disguised as a living room or decorated, a choice the review's authors judged to have been made without evidence. Certainty: very low.

set.plain: In surveys, people who felt safe and supported during a trip reported a little less fear and fewer difficulties, but they rated both afterwards. The only study among these that asked people beforehand found only a weak, uncertain link between feeling good about the place and the people and how the trip went, and no detectable difference for retreats or settings designed for therapy. No study put people in different settings on purpose to compare them: a review of 25 clinical trials found none that did, and the trials set up their rooms and staff in very different ways.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, giving very low (the floor). Status mixed: four independent studies; support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys (Perkins et al.; the no-support attribution in Simonsson et al.) and the untested party comparison points the same way, but blaming the people around showed no such link, and the one prospective study found only a non-significant trend for its setting rating (and a weak link with well-being two weeks later) and no association for a retreat or therapeutic setting; recall at the same sitting may explain part of the difference, but no study has shown that it does. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2), and the associations it showed for trust and a therapeutic setting were not significant in the fuller report; a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) found no trial comparing settings up to December 2023. A trial analysis in which the quality of the therapeutic alliance correlated with emotional breakthrough and mystical-type experience (Murphy et al., 2022), cited by that review, has not been read.

no study read here compared sessions with and without music, or with different music.

no study read here compared sessions with and without music, and the one randomized comparison of two kinds of music, in 10 people, found no detectable difference, with intervals too wide to rule one out.
statement
Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

In the one randomized comparison of music (Strickland et al., 2021; a published correction to the article has not been read), 10 adults who smoked (8 men; mean age 51), in an open-label pilot of psilocybin to help people stop smoking, each had one session with a Western classical playlist and one with an 'overtone-based' playlist of instruments such as singing bowls, gongs and didgeridoo, in random, counterbalanced order, wearing an eye mask and headphones, with a lower dose in the first session than in the second for all but one (study conditions; the analysis adjusted for dose). Mystical-type scores (MEQ30, self-rated at the end of each session and printed on a 0-to-1 scale) averaged 0.68 with the overtone playlist and 0.52 with the classical one, a difference of 0.16 (standardized 0.57; editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36, from rounded figures) that was not statistically significant (p = 0.107); Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores were almost the same (0.33 against 0.34; standardized difference −0.11, editors' interval about −0.73 to 0.51; p = 0.74). The data therefore fit anything from slightly lower to much higher mystical-type scores with the overtone playlist, and from a moderate fall to a moderate rise in challenge. About a quarter of the classical playlist's tracks were also on the overtone playlist, about an hour of each person's own chosen music was played in every session, the overtone playlist lost three tracks after the first three people, and everyone knew which music they heard. Six of the ten then chose the overtone playlist for a third session; smoking abstinence at the end of treatment (5 of 6 who chose it against 2 of 4 who chose the classical one; editors' Fisher p = 0.50) compares people who chose differently after hearing both playlists, so it cannot show an effect of the music. In a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025), 16 trials played a set playlist through headphones, one alternated music and silence, two allowed no music, and none compared settings; trials treating substance use, such as the smoking pilot, were outside its scope. An older study that compared five musical conditions, no music among them, during LSD sessions for alcohol use (Gaston and Eagle, 1970) is described by Strickland et al. as finding no significant differences, in a between-subject, partly non-random design without an objective clinical outcome; it has not been read here. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

set.plain: In one small study of 19 patients given psilocybin in a clinic, almost all said the music helped at times, and about half said it sometimes made things harder. Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression, but both were measured at the same time, a week later, so feeling better may have coloured how they described the music. In a trial of 10 people, each heard classical music in one psilocybin session and music of gongs and singing bowls in another, in random order; how mystical or difficult the sessions felt did not clearly differ, but the trial was too small to rule out a real difference. None of the studies we read compared sessions with and without music.
set.population: Patients with treatment-resistant depression in an open-label psilocybin trial (19); adults who smoked, in an open-label psilocybin smoking-cessation pilot (10, with the order of two playlists randomized); and US adults who had used classic psychedelics in an online panel (613)
set.exposure: Music played during psilocybin sessions: one standard playlist (with one exception), as patients described it a week later; a Western classical or an overtone-based playlist, in randomized order within each person; disagreeable music named as associated with a most challenging experience
set.comparator: No study had a session without music: the other playlist in the same person (randomized comparison); patients who described the music less favourably; panel respondents who did not name the music
set.outcome: What patients said the music did; fall in self-rated depression (QIDS) one week after; mystical-type experience (MEQ30) and challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) self-rated after each session; smoking abstinence by chosen playlist; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the days or weeks after
set.magnitude: Kaelen et al. (2018), n = 19: welcome influences 18 of 19, unwelcome 10 of 19; QIDS fall with music liking r = 0.60 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.83, editors'), resonance 0.59, openness 0.57; drug intensity r = 0.004 (−0.45 to 0.46). Simonsson et al. (2023): disagreeable music named by 30 of 613, not associated with challenge (beta 0.05, p = 0.19) or, imprecisely, with later thoughts or attempts of harm (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21); changing the music ticked as helpful by 99 of 613. Strickland et al. (2021), n = 10, randomized sessions 1 and 2: MEQ30 0.68 (SD 0.20) overtone against 0.52 (SD 0.21) Western classical, dz 0.57, p = 0.107 (dose-adjusted b = 0.14, p = 0.108); editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36 (dz about −0.12 to 1.23); CEQ 0.33 (SD 0.20) against 0.34 (SD 0.22), dz −0.11, p = 0.74 (editors' dz interval about −0.73 to 0.51). Abstinence by chosen playlist, not randomized: 5 of 6 (overtone) against 2 of 4 (classical) at the end of treatment and 4 of 6 against 2 of 4 at long-term follow-up (editors' Fisher p = 0.50 and 1.0).

risk_of_bias.note: The randomized genre comparison has some concerns (card sc_strickland_2021): open label, self-ratings by participants who knew which music they heard, the overtone playlist changed after three participants, no registered analysis plan, and period effects untested. The music-experience ratings in the depression trial come from interviews at the same time point as the outcome, with no adjustment and no music-free condition (card sc_kaelen_2018, overall very high), and the panel survey's attributions are retrospective (sc_simonsson_2023); both are worded only as associations.

inconsistency.note: The sources answer different questions (two playlists compared, how patients experienced one playlist, music named in a survey).

indirectness.note: The randomized comparison tested two genres, not music against silence, with about a quarter of the classical tracks shared and each person's own music in every session, in 10 people in a smoking-cessation pilot; the other sources are a hospital trial of patients with depression and a US panel.

imprecision.note: 10 people in the randomized comparison, with intervals from slightly lower to much higher mystical-type scores and from a moderate fall to a moderate rise in challenge; 19 patients for the main correlation (interval 0.20 to 0.83); the panel's harm estimate for music rests on 30 people (interval 0.87 to 8.21).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; no registered analysis plan is reported for the genre comparison.

grade.reasoning: Rated from the one randomized comparison, the best evidence on whether the music itself changes a session: randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias, one for indirectness and two for imprecision, giving very low (the floor). The correlational evidence on how patients experienced the music (Kaelen et al., 2018) is very low on its own, as before (low, minus two for risk of bias and one for imprecision). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither an effect of the music nor its absence can be shown with precision. Status single study: each question rests on one small study (two genres compared in 10 people; the music experience and the fall in depression in 19 patients); the panel survey adds only null associations, one very imprecise, for music named as associated with a difficult experience. A systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low) found none that compared settings, music included; trials treating substance use were outside its scope. A published correction to Strickland et al. (2021; doi 10.1021/acsptsci.1c00119) was not among the files and has not been read, so any figure it changes is unchecked. The only comparison with a no-music condition in psychedelic sessions that these sources mention, a 1970 quasi-randomized study of LSD sessions (Gaston and Eagle), is known only from Strickland et al.'s description and has not been read. A 2025 opinion article argues against music in therapy settings and notes that no controlled study compares music with silence; it has no card.

replace: statement

As described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session goes. The review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, all in patients in clinical or trial settings.

Evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session feels or how well the treatment works; one randomized trial found a smaller rise in blood pressure with music. In that trial (Greenway et al., 2024; Montreal, 2021 to 2022; registered), 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression, accepted for a clinical course of six intravenous ketamine infusions over 4 weeks (treatment conditions), were randomly assigned to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion (15) or to usual care without music (17). Across 181 infusions, systolic blood pressure rose from the start to the end of each infusion by 7.4 mm Hg less with music than without (95% CI 2.9 to 12.0; a mean rise of roughly 11.5 against 18.5 mm Hg, read from the figure), while diastolic pressure did not differ detectably (0.8 mm Hg less; the printed interval, −1.59 to 3.18, appears to have its signs transposed); no serious adverse events were recorded. The letter reports nothing on how the sessions felt, dissociation or depression (left for later papers), nor how many patients in each group needed treatment for raised blood pressure (the authors cite up to 20% of patients on intravenous ketamine for depression in general); the comparison was with no music, without a sound or attention control, so the music cannot be separated from attention or expectation; and one patient given usual care was left out of the analysis without a stated reason. Before that trial, as described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), 14 studies of music with ketamine had been published, all in patients in clinical or trial settings.

set.plain: In one trial of 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression who had ketamine through a drip in hospital, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less in those picked at random to hear music than in those who heard none. The trial has not yet reported how the sessions felt or whether depression improved. An earlier review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, mostly with other medicines during surgery or tests, where music often went with less worry or pain; it found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression. So it is not known whether music changes how a ketamine session feels.
set.population: 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression receiving a clinical course of intravenous ketamine in Montreal (one randomized trial), and patients given ketamine or esketamine in clinical settings (anaesthesia, sedation, depression and alcohol-use-disorder treatment) in 14 earlier studies gathered by a scoping review
set.exposure: Curated music throughout each 40-minute ketamine infusion (trial); music (or, in one study, recordings of mothers' voices) before, during or after ketamine or esketamine (review)
set.comparator: Usual care without music (trial); no music (headphones with no recording, or a blank soundtrack) in most procedural trials and in the one comparison of ketamine alone; no comparison in the case reports and interview studies (review)
set.outcome: Rise in systolic and diastolic blood pressure from the start to the end of each infusion (trial); anxiety, pain, emergence reactions, sedative use, dissociation and how the session was experienced (review)

risk_of_bias.note: The trial (card sc_greenway_2024), RoB 2 some concerns: open label by necessity; sequence generation and allocation concealment not described; one usual-care patient excluded from analysis without a stated reason; more infusions missing without music (8 against 3), handled by inverse-probability weighting; who measured blood pressure, and whether they knew the group, not described. The review's studies were not appraised by the review and cannot be appraised here, and its highlights state benefits that its limitations disclaim (card sc_kheirkhah_2024).

inconsistency.note: Directions vary between the review's procedural trials (one null, one with more dreams or emergence reactions), as the statement says; the trial measured a different outcome.

indirectness.note: For the question asked (how a session feels, or how well treatment works), the trial reports only blood pressure, and its comparison was no music without a sound or attention control; the review's evidence is second-hand (METHODS §6.3) and mostly from ketamine given with other sedatives during procedures, often in children, and the only controlled ketamine-alone study used mothers' voices, partly spoken.

imprecision.note: One trial of 32 patients (interval for the smaller systolic rise 2.9 to 12.0 mm Hg); for how sessions feel, only small studies, mostly without a comparison group.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the trial was registered (NCT04701866), but its registry record and protocol supplement were not read, so the reported outcome was not compared with the registered one.

grade.reasoning: The best evidence is now one randomized trial, which starts high, but it answers only blood pressure: on its own, the smaller systolic rise with music would rate low (high, minus one for risk of bias and one for imprecision). For how a session feels, the evidence is still the review's small, mostly procedural studies seen second-hand (low, minus risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low). Rated for the claim as worded: down one each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low. Status single study: one randomized trial for blood pressure, and, for ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparison of listening with not listening (46 children under anaesthesia hearing recordings of their mothers' voices), seen through one review. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review; its new anchors still need a second reader's check. The trial's secondary outcomes, deferred to later publications, have not been seen.

replace: statement
In one randomized, double-blind crossover trial in a laboratory, 18 healthy adults

In healthy volunteers in laboratory studies, evidence is insufficient to say whether CBD taken with, or shortly before, THC changes THC's effects, compared with the same amount of THC taken the same way without CBD: results differ between studies and outcomes, and no pattern by amount, route or ratio has been found. A systematic review of such studies (Freeman et al., 2019; searched to February 2019; 16 studies in 23 articles published from 1974 to 2019, 13 crossover and 3 parallel-group, 466 healthy volunteers in all, almost all of whom had used cannabis before, mostly occasionally; nothing pooled; the editors rate confidence in the review critically low) covers THC swallowed, injected into a vein, smoked, vaporised or sprayed in the mouth, in widely different amounts and ratios. As summarized there, most studies found no significant difference with CBD in THC's blood levels (most of eight studies; one vaporised study of 14 people found a higher peak with CBD), in the rise in heart rate (no difference in nine of ten studies) or in how intoxicated people felt (seven of nine; two small studies, one smoked and one by mouth, found less). Reports of less anxiety or fewer psychosis-like effects with CBD come mainly from four studies in which THC was swallowed or injected into a vein: groups of 5 given THC by mouth (the most intense grade of effects, such as panic, in 4 of 5 after THC alone against 3 of 15 with CBD added; no statistical test reported in the review), a crossover of 8 people given both by mouth, a pseudo-randomised crossover of 6 people given both into a vein (3 of whom had psychosis-like effects after THC alone), and a parallel trial of 48 people given THC into a vein after CBD or a placebo by mouth, in which the average rise in psychosis-like symptoms did not differ although fewer of those given CBD had a clinically significant rise; the review's discussion nonetheless describes three of these studies as showing significantly fewer people with extreme anxiety or psychosis-like effects. With vaporised THC, a 48-person crossover found no difference in psychosis-like effects, and in the 14-person study anxiety rose 15 minutes after THC with and without CBD and was still raised an hour later only without it. Results on memory, attention and movement tasks went in both directions. In a later randomized, double-blind crossover trial in a laboratory, 18 healthy adults

set.plain: Lab studies disagree on whether CBD changes how THC feels. In most of 16 older studies, adding CBD made no clear difference to how high people felt, to their heart rate or to THC in their blood. A few small studies, in which THC was swallowed or injected, found less anxiety or fewer paranoid feelings with CBD; studies with vaporised THC found little or no difference. In one later trial, 18 healthy adults who ate THC with a large amount of CBD had more THC in their blood, felt the drug more, felt sicker and had more trouble with memory and simple tasks, but other test medicines, including a sedative, were also given. No pattern by amount or by way of taking it has been found.

risk_of_bias.note: The review's 16 studies are seen only through a review the editors rate critically low on AMSTAR 2 (card sc_freeman_2019: English-language, peer-reviewed-only search; risk of bias not weighed in its conclusions); its own ratings (10 low, 6 some concerns) include a pseudo-randomised study rated low, and its text and table disagree in several places. The later trial, RoB 2 some concerns (card sc_zamarripa_2023): only completers analysed after 4 of 22 randomized dropped out and were replaced; 36 outcomes without correction; the abstract, text and table disagree on several results, and many printed effect sizes do not match the printed data.

inconsistency.note: Directions differ: most studies found no difference on most outcomes; four small studies with THC swallowed or injected reported less anxiety or fewer psychosis-like effects; one vaporised study found a shorter-lasting rise in anxiety but more divided-attention impairment with CBD; the later oral trial found higher blood THC and stronger, mostly unwanted effects; the review found no pattern by route, dose or ratio that would explain the differences.

indirectness.note: The review's studies are second-hand (METHODS §6.3); all used single doses in screened healthy volunteers, most with occasional use, with laboratory routes, amounts and ratios that rarely match products people use; in the later trial, whole-plant extracts carrying other cannabinoids and a probe cocktail including the sedative midazolam, whose levels are not reported.

imprecision.note: Six of the review's studies had 4 to 8 people per condition and nothing was pooled; the later trial had 18 people, with task differences at P = .049 and .04 and printed intervals that cannot be relied on.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed: the review judged it low because studies reported a mix of significant and non-significant results, which is not a method of detecting it; the later trial was registered (NCT04201197).

grade.reasoning: Randomized within-person and parallel laboratory comparisons start high (METHODS §6.3); the review's studies are seen only second-hand. Down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low (the floor). The rise in blood THC and 11-OH-THC in the later trial, on its own, is large, objective and precise and would rate low (high, minus risk of bias and indirectness). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither an effect of CBD on THC's acute effects nor its absence can be shown with precision. Status mixed: 17 studies with inconsistent findings and no adequate explanation of the differences. The review (Freeman et al., 2019) is used only for what each study reported, described by route and size, and not for a general claim that CBD protects against THC's anxiety or psychosis-like effects: its discussion calls three studies' results significant where its own summaries give no test for two and no difference in the average for the third. Not yet read: the primary studies, later randomized studies of THC with and without CBD on the reading list (Arkell et al., 2020; Lawn et al., 2023) and a 2026 meta-analysis of blood THC with CBD (Chester et al.).

change: Round pdf-2026-11-01: AI reader 320 (claim writer) added Freeman et al. (2019), the systematic review of 16 laboratory studies of THC with and without CBD (466 healthy volunteers, 1974 to 2019; nothing pooled; AMSTAR 2 critically low), from AI reader 300's first-pass study card (seven anchors, ai-located; a second reader must check them). The claim now answers the mixing question across all the studies read: most found no difference in blood THC, heart rate or intoxication; the reports of less anxiety or fewer psychosis-like effects come mainly from four small studies with THC swallowed or injected into a vein (groups of 5, 8 and 6 people, and a 48-person trial in which the average did not differ), the review's description of them as significant goes beyond its own summaries, and the studies with vaporised THC found little or no difference; the Zamarripa trial, kept unchanged, is now the later study whose direction and conditions differ. Amounts appear only in the magnitude, as study conditions; nothing suggests combining the two. Relation changed from is-associated-with to insufficient-evidence and status from single study to mixed (17 studies with inconsistent findings, no pattern by route, dose or ratio); GRADE now down one for inconsistency as well (certainty unchanged, very low). Population, exposure, comparator, outcome, magnitude and plain text updated.
